current_answer: AI adopters hired less in Denmark: firms first reporting AI use in 2023 had employment growth 11% below non-adopters by late 2025 relative to their earlier trend, driven by lower recruitment and concentrated in smaller firms. That is a serious adoption-linked hiring warning, not proof that AI caused every missing job or that an economy-wide layoff wave has begun. California’s latest exposure-based unemployment-claims tracker moved slightly down, not up, while broad U.S. posting and Nordic results still limit a universal verdict. The risk now looks more concentrated and outcome-specific—not imaginary, but not a forecast for your job.

catalogue_card.question: What changed in the AI jobs evidence?
catalogue_card.text: A Danish study links reported AI adoption to slower hiring at smaller firms. It is closer to the cause than an exposure score, but it is not an economy-wide layoff verdict.

summary: A Danish firm-record study finds slower employment growth after reported AI adoption, driven by lower recruitment and concentrated in smaller firms.
California’s latest high-exposure unemployment-claims update did not show a surge, so hiring restraint and unemployment must remain separate.
The decisive next tests will replicate firm-level adoption studies across countries and follow recruitment into wages, separations and unemployment.
uncertainty: Adoption is non-random in the Danish study, so firm differences and concurrent changes can still explain part of the association.
Denmark and California measure different outcomes and treatments; neither finding predicts a reader’s own job.
U.S. early-career results remain exposure-based, with rival explanations including remote work and pre-trends.
